titleEn: Laws of Hammurabi — §52–65: crops, dikes and orchards (xv 1 – xvi 77)
part: Laws §52–65 · crops, dikes and orchards (Col. xv 1 – xvi 77)
about: Fourteen laws on the damage one farmer can do to another’s crop, and on the date-orchard. A tenant whose field yields nothing is still held to his contract (§52). Then water: a man who lets his dike decay or leaves his ditch open and floods the fields round about must replace the grain he destroyed — and if he cannot, he and his goods are sold and the farmers of the district share the price (§53–56). Then sheep: a shepherd who grazes his flock on a man’s field without leave pays in grain, and more if he does it after the flocks have been brought in from the fields (§57–58). The last laws turn to orchards: a fine for felling another man’s tree (§59), and the contract between a landowner and the gardener who plants his field as a date-orchard or tends one already planted — the four unproductive years, the division of the fifth, the land left unplanted, the pollination of the palms and the share of the crop (§60–65). After §65 the stele was chiselled smooth in antiquity — five columns by Harper’s count; the laws that stood there follow in the next parts from other copies.

sentences.l: If the-tenant in the-field grain or sesame not has-caused-to-be, his-contracts he-shall-not-change.
sentences.i: If the tenant did not raise grain or sesame in the field, he may not change his contract.
sentences.n: The last of the tenant laws (§42–47): a bad crop does not undo the lease. riksātum, the “bindings” you met in §47, are the terms of the contract; inni is enûm “to change” in the present, and ul inni is a flat statement of law: “he shall not alter” them — he still owes what he agreed. uštabši is the Š-stem perfect of bašûm again (§42, §49). Here the grain-sign carries a phonetic complement: the stele writes ŠE-am, the sign ŠE followed by am to tell you to read šeʾam (Harper prints še-am).

sentences.l: If a-man for his-dike to-strengthen his-arm let-drop and his-dike not he-strengthened, and in his-dike a-breach has-opened and the-irrigated-land the-water he-has-let-carry-off,
sentences.i: If a man neglected to keep his dike strong and did not strengthen it, and a breach opened in his dike and he let the water carry away the irrigated land,
sentences.n: The water laws begin. kārum (Harper kâru) is the dike or embankment that holds the water back, written with the single sign KAR, the TE sign with extra wedges (Harper’s List of Signs no. 147: kar, kâru). ana kārišu dunnunim is ana with an infinitive, “for the strengthening of his dike”: dunnunum is the D-stem of danānum “to be strong”, and udannin, in the next clause, its preterite. aḫšu iddi, “he let his arm drop,” is the idiom for negligence you met at §44. pītum is a breach (Harper bi-tum: the BI sign also stands for pí), and ittepti the N-stem perfect of petûm, “has opened.” ugārum, written A.GÀR, is the irrigated land of a district, shared by many farmers; mê uštābil is wabālum “to carry” in the Š-stem perfect, “he has made the water carry off,” with two objects, the land and the water. The stone is damaged in XV 8–14: Harper draws the lost signs in outline and brackets them — KAR in line 8, -un-nu- in line 9, id-di-ma in line 10, the -šu of KAR-šu in lines 11 and 13, -ni-in-ma in line 12, -ip-ti in line 14 — Harper’s restorations, supported by the same words repeated in the lines around them.

sentences.l: the-man who in his-dike the-breach was-opened, the-grain which he-caused-to-be-lost shall-replace.
sentences.i: the man in whose dike the breach opened shall replace the grain he caused to be lost.
sentences.n: The penalty repeats the case in short as a relative clause: awīlum ša ina kārišu pītum ippetû, “the man in whose dike the breach was opened” — ippetû (Harper ib-bi-tu-u) is the N-stem preterite of petûm with the subjunctive -u that every verb in a ša-clause takes. uḫalliqu is ḫalāqum “to be lost” in the D-stem, “he made (it) be lost,” again subjunctive. iriab is riābum “to replace,” as in §8 and §23. The plate shows the sign ḪAL in u-ḫal-li-ḳu (Harper’s List of Signs no. 2).

sentences.l: If grain to-replace not he-is-able, him and his-goods for silver they-shall-give, and
sentences.i: If he is unable to replace the grain, he and his goods shall be sold for silver, and
sentences.n: If he cannot pay, the loss falls on his person: he is sold. šuāti is the independent pronoun “him” (the accusative of šū); bīšum is movable property, “goods.” ana kaspim nadānum, “to give for silver,” is to sell; the plural inaddinū is the impersonal “they” of the authorities. riābam is the infinitive of riābum, and lā ileʾʾi “he is not able” is leʾûm, as in §28.

sentences.l: the-sons of-the-irrigated-land whose grain the-water carried-off shall-divide (it).
sentences.i: the farmers of the irrigated land whose grain the water carried away shall share the proceeds.
sentences.n: DUMU A.GÀR{meš}, “the sons of the irrigated land,” are the farmers of the district who share its water: DUMU “son” (mārum) in its sense “member of a group,” A.GÀR = ugārum, and MEŠ, the plural marker, cut after the whole phrase — the sign ME with three corner-wedges (Harper’s List of Signs no. 185). Harper prints the group as one word, mâr+ugarê. mû “water” is plural in Akkadian, so the verb is too: mû ublū, “the water carried off.” ša šeʾšunu, “whose grain” — ša with a suffix on the noun that follows. The price of the man and his goods goes to the neighbours he flooded.

sentences.l: If a-shepherd for the-plants the-sheep to-make-eat with the-owner of-the-field not has-agreed, and
sentences.i: If a shepherd has not come to an agreement with the owner of a field to graze his sheep on its plants,
sentences.n: The grazing laws. rēʾûm “shepherd” is written PA.LU, two signs read together as SIPA (Harper: rêʾu). ṣēnū “sheep (and goats), the flock” is written U₈.UDU{ḫi.a}: the ewe-sign U₈, the sheep-sign UDU, and the plural marker ḪI.A. sentences.l: If after the-sheep from the-irrigated-land have-come-up (and) the-bands of-completion on the-city-gate have-been-hung,
sentences.i: If, after the sheep have come up from the irrigated fields and the bands that mark the end of grazing have been hung up at the city gate,
sentences.n: A harder case: grazing after the season has closed. ištu “after.” ṣēnū is a feminine plural, and so is its verb: īteliānim is elûm “to go up” in the perfect, feminine plural ītelia (ītelâ), with the ventive -nim “hither” — the flocks have come up from the fields into town. kannū gamartim is literally “the bands of completion” (kannum “band, tie”; gamartum “end”): something hung at the city gate as a public sign that the grazing is over. The words are clear, the custom is not; ittaḫlalū looks like the N-stem perfect, plural, of a verb ḫalālum, “have been hung up,” a meaning inferred from the context. Harper prints ga ma-ar tim without hyphens; on the plate it is one word, GA-MA-AR-TIM.

sentences.l: the-shepherd the-field he-made-eat shall-guard and at the-harvest for-10 GAN.E 60 GUR of-grain to the-owner of-the-field he-shall-measure-out.
sentences.i: the shepherd shall keep watch over the field he grazed, and at harvest he shall measure out to the owner of the field sixty kor of grain for every ten bur.
sentences.n: eqel ušākilu, “the field (that) he grazed,” is a relative clause without ša: the noun stands in the construct and the verb takes the subjunctive. Harper prints eḳlum, a nominative, but A.ŠÀ shows no case ending and the grammar asks for the construct. inaṣṣarma, from naṣārum “to guard”: the field is in his charge until harvest. The penalty is sixty kor per ten bur, three times §57’s. Sixty is one vertical wedge, the same stroke as “one” at the next sexagesimal place (Harper’s LX). The column changes at the stele’s line XVI 1.

sentences.l: ½ mina of-silver he-shall-weigh-out.
sentences.i: he shall weigh out half a mina of silver.
sentences.n: A fixed fine in silver. The half is one sign, a horizontal crossed by a vertical (Harper’s List of Numerals: ½); it is written 1/2 here and drawn with the MAŠ sign, “half” — the identification of the character is ours, Harper gives only the shape. Its Akkadian, mišil “half (of),” is a reconstruction. ma-na, the mina (sixty shekels, about 500 g): Harper writes it as a plain syllabic word here, where §24 read the same two signs as the logogram MA.NA. išaqqal is šaqālum “to weigh out,” i.e. to pay; its last sign is GAL, read qal (Harper ḳal).

sentences.n: The gardener, NU.{giš}KIRI₆, is “the man of the orchard” in Sumerian. sentences.l: the-gardener the-orchard planted, four years the-orchard he-shall-raise;
sentences.i: and the gardener planted the orchard, he shall tend the orchard for four years;
sentences.n: izqup, preterite of zaqāpum, still belongs to the condition; the rule starts with urabba, rabûm “to grow” in the D-stem, “he shall raise (it)” — the verb used of bringing up a child in §29. MU 4{kam} is the year-sign, four wedges, and KAM: here a stretch of time, said erbe šanātim “four years” (a reconstruction), like ana MU 3{kam} at §44. Young palms bear nothing; the gardener carries those years.

sentences.l: if (it is) furrow-land, the-yield of-the-field of the-years which it-was-left-lying the-gardener to the-owner of-the-field like its-neighbour shall-measure-out,
sentences.i: then, if it is ploughland, the gardener shall measure out to the owner the field’s yield for the years it lay neglected, at the rate of the neighbouring field,
sentences.n: A second šumma inside the first: the case divides by the kind of land. AB.SÍN (Harper abšênum) is absinnum, the furrow — ploughed, sown ground, against the waste land of §63; “if (it is) furrow” is a verbless clause. The second sign is damaged on the stone and Harper draws part of it in outline; it is read here as SÍN, a compound of the grain-sign ŠE and the sign NAGA — the identification is uncertain. bilat eqlim, “the yield of the field,” uses the tribute-sign GÚN as in §45. ša šanātim ša innadû, “of the years in which it lay neglected”: šanātum is the plural of šattum, and innadû nadûm in the N-stem, subjunctive.

sentences.i: as long as he holds the orchard, the gardener shall give the owner two-thirds of its yield and take one third himself.
sentences.n: adi kirâm ṣabtu, “as long as he holds the orchard” — ṣabtu is the stative of ṣabātum “to seize, hold,” with the subjunctive -u after adi. Harper prints kirûm, which makes the orchard the subject (“as long as the orchard is held”); the logogram shows no case and the stative allows either reading. We take the gardener as the one who holds it, with the orchard as object, kirâm. šittīn is “two-thirds,” šaluštum “one third” (the widow’s third of §29). šū, “he,” is stressed: he himself.

sentences.l: the-gardener the-yield of-the-orchard according-to its-neighbour [shall-measure-out].
sentences.i: the gardener [shall measure out] the orchard’s yield at the rate of the neighbouring orchard.
sentences.n: He makes good the shortfall, judged by the orchard next door. The last line, XVI 77, is lost: Harper’s plate draws nothing for it (the column on the plate ends with line 76), and his transliteration restores the whole word in brackets, [i-ma-ad-da-ad], the verb that closes the parallel §55 and §62. The signs shown for it are that restoration, not a reading of the stone. Below it the stone has been cut away — five columns, the laws Harper numbers §66–99 — and the code resumes, from other copies, in the next parts.
